content.title: The parts
content.text: Every piece of the digit reader has a standard name, the same in every paper and library. A neuron, also called a unit, is the adder with a squash of pill 02; there are 58 here. Neurons stand in layers: an input layer of 64 pixels, two hidden layers of 32 and 16, an output layer of 10. The knob on a wire is a weight; the lift inside a neuron is its bias. Together they are the parameters, 2,778 of them: 2,720 weights and 58 biases. The shape plus its numbers is the model, and this shape, rows of neurons each fed by the whole row before, is a multilayer perceptron, MLP, the class Part 2 builds.

content.title: Forward
content.text: Running a picture through the model is the forward pass; doing it with a trained model to get an answer is inference, and the answer is its prediction. Inside neuron 10 of the first row, the sum before the squash, 0.2353, is the pre-activation. The squash is the activation function, tanh here, ReLU in most networks today, and what leaves, 0.2311, is the activation. The ten raw scores at the end are the logits; softmax turns them into scores that add up to 100%, so each can be read as the model’s confidence. For this 7 the top score goes to 9, at 99.15%: the prediction is wrong.

content.title: The loss
content.text: The right answer attached to a picture is its label: 7. The loss function turns a prediction and a label into one number for how wrong: this one is cross-entropy, minus the log of the score given to the right digit, −log(0.24%) = 6.03 for this picture. Averaged over the 3,823 pictures of the training set, the ones the knobs learned from, it is 0.0416, pill 07’s bowl. The 1,797 pictures of the test set were never used for learning; the share it gets right there, 95.9%, is its accuracy, and doing well on pictures never seen is generalisation, the point of the whole exercise.

content.title: The slopes
content.text: How the loss moves when one knob turns is that knob’s derivative, pill 08’s slope. It is written ∂loss/∂w, the curly d saying that every other knob is held still. All 2,778 slopes together, one list, is the gradient. It points the way the loss rises fastest; the recipe walks the other way. At the trained knobs the gradient over the training pictures is small, mean 0.0011, knob A’s own slope −0.0010: the field is dim because little is left to fix on the training pictures.

content.title: Backward
content.text: Computing the whole gradient in one walk from the loss back to the inputs is the backward pass, or backpropagation; the maths it leans on is the chain rule of pill 09, slopes multiplying along a path and adding across paths. What pill 09 called blame, the slope of the loss against a neuron’s sum, is what code stores in a field named grad: for neuron 10 reading this 7, 1.0426, times the squash slope 0.9466 already in it, times the pixel 0.625 gives its weight’s slope 0.6516. A program that performs the backward pass for any forward computation is automatic differentiation, autograd. Every library has one; Part 2 writes one by hand.

content.title: The step
content.text: Pill 11’s rule, new = old − 0.05 × slope, is gradient descent. Taking the slope on a mini-batch, 32 pictures instead of all 3,823, makes it stochastic gradient descent, SGD, the default of the whole field. The 0.05 is the learning rate. One pass over all the training pictures is an epoch, 60 here; one step is an iteration, 120 per epoch, 7,200 in all. The numbers chosen by hand rather than learned, learning rate, batch size, number of epochs, are hyperparameters. A library’s optimizer is this rule, packaged, often with refinements.

content.title: One picture, all the names
content.text: A model of 2,778 parameters in layers; a forward pass to logits and softmax; a loss against the label; a gradient by backpropagation; a step of gradient descent at a learning rate, over mini-batches, for 60 epochs. Nothing on this page is new; only the words are, and they are the words of every paper and every library. Part 2 builds the engine behind the backward pass by hand, micrograd, in about a hundred lines, and uses these names throughout.
